players.product: retail colocation & interconnection (IBX data centers, Equinix Fabric) and xScale hyperscale data centers

quarterly_data.signal: Head of Investor Relations Ryan Burke quantified the secured pipeline behind the raised long-term outlook: 'we've talked about having 3 gigawatts of land and power essentially secured, meaning it's either signed and secured or it's maybe a page flip away from being signed and secured', and said that most of what appears in Equinix's reported pipeline carries 'pretty good degree of certainty around it getting executed'. Guy Danskine (MD, Americas West) added that 'The power that we've announced, we have largely under control', and that Equinix is not shocking utilities - it shows up asking for 60 megawatts over a defined period rather than '300 megawatts tomorrow', which he said is what is 'really causing the congestion in the system'.
quarterly_data.figure: 3 gigawatts of land and power essentially secured; 60 megawatts requests vs 300 megawatts tomorrow

quarterly_data.signal: Next-generation design point disclosed: Danskine said the main difference in new builds is power density - 'What customers are now showing up for in our next generation builds is they are wanting densities of 40 to 60 kilowatts-plus per cabinet. That fundamentally changes how we think about designing the site.' On liquid cooling: 'It is not going to be the be all and end all 5 years from now, but the fact is it is going to be taking up a larger percentage of our sites, and so we are building now with that thinking in mind' - current facilities worldwide are being built so customers can 'show up, plug and play' with liquid cooling.
quarterly_data.figure: densities of 40 to 60 kilowatts-plus per cabinet

quarterly_data.signal: Texas regulatory exposure quantified. Danskine: 'For Equinix, I would think about it more like Dallas, not Texas' - the West Texas activity drawing government scrutiny is not where Equinix plays. On the Texas governor's halt on new data-center expansion: 'take for example, Dallas, we're looking at a 60-megawatt build there. The threshold that the government have released is 75 megawatts.' Earlier in the same session, on the governor's action, he said 'A number of our assets sit underneath that threshold, including our expansion.' Equinix anchors everything in that metro to the Infomart asset acquired '7 or 8 years ago' because proximity 'drives just fundamentally stronger economics', has several plots of land under control there, and remains 'incredibly bullish on Dallas as one of our top markets globally', helped by financial services moving in and relatively better power availability.
quarterly_data.figure: Dallas 60-megawatt build vs a 75 megawatts government threshold

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity is the number one operating priority and a meaningful part of it comes from existing assets rather than new builds. Danskine: end-of-life equipment such as power distribution units or CRAH units has 'a 10 to 15 year refresh cycle', so through natural refresh Equinix swaps in next-generation gear that is 'either twice as efficient or twice as capable or maybe half the form factor', unlocking greater power density in older facilities. Scope of the lever runs from individual asset optimisation up to M&A within the region. Customers are also becoming more 'fungible' about location because capacity is not available exactly where and when they want it, and are splitting workloads across facilities in the same metro.
quarterly_data.figure: 10 to 15 year refresh cycle on PDUs and CRAH units; replacement equipment twice as efficient / twice as capable / half the form factor

quarterly_data.signal: Where the AI workload actually lands for Equinix: Danskine said a network density is forming around neoclouds and LLM providers similar to what happened with cloud - 'The focus for some of them have gone from where is the compute that I can get access, to now how do I distribute that compute to my customers' - and 'a ton of that networking is going to happen in and around Equinix'. Equinix maintains a per-metro target customer list and is intentional about capturing 'the network component at a minimum' of those customers: 'To be clear, this isn't the training side of things. This is from inferencing forward in the stack.' Metro example: the Chicago expansion 'down to Manuka, and that is a hybrid xScale campus', with significant enterprise pull-through expected and workloads split between downtown (high-frequency trading), Elk Grove and Manuka (back office). Burke added that there 'typically tends to be a bit of a lag between deployment of space and power and the interconnect associated with those', so the interconnection outlook is favourable.
